Reasons for order:

NARIB AJ:

[1]	The court is seized with two applications to amend. Both applications concern amendment of the pleas, - the first one, under case number INT-HC-AMDPLEA-2025/00017 is by the third parties, to amend the plea to the third-party notice filed by the defendant, - and the second one, under case number INT-HC-AMDPLEA-2025/00138 is by the defendant to further amend the amended plea to the plaintiff’s particulars of claim. Only the plaintiff opposes the applications.

[2]	The amendments sought seek to raise similar issues and the objections thereto to are in some material respects, also similar. Therefore, both applications were heard together on 17 June 2025, and it is convenient that both be disposed of in a single judgement. I shall proceed to do so.

[3]	The notice of intention to amend on behalf of the third parties was filed on 18 October 2024 and the one on behalf of the defendant was filed on 8 January 2025. The pleadings in the application brought by the third parties closed on 27 February 2025, whereas in the application brought by the defendant, such pleadings closed on 12 March 2025.

[4]	Both applications were initially set down for 16 May 2025, but could not be heard on that day, and the hearing was moved to 17 May 2025, for me to hear the matters, which I did, and upon which I reserved judgment, to be delivered on 8 July 2025.

[5]	I set out the above chronology, just to show that even an application to amend can delay a matter for more than six months and that care must be taken when amendments are initiated, and objections are taken to such amendments. In this matter, in view of the position I take, regarding the amendments, the plaintiff who amongst others, objects to the amendments on the basis that it is brought late in the proceedings and will delay the matter by reopening of the pleadings, is responsible for the further delay in the ultimate finalisation of the proceedings. In my view the amendments should have been conceded or agreed to because the objections taken, in each case, are without merit.

[6]	The amendment sought by the third parties, as I have said above, relates to the plea to the third-party notice which was filed by the defendants. In addition to correcting some typographical errors, the amendment seeks to introduce two additional defences, one aimed at impugning the power, authority, or ability of the defendant to bind the Joint Venture between the defendant and the third parties to the contract entered into between the defendant and the plaintiff, with the additional assertion that the said contract was in any event objectively impossible to perform for a miner at the place from which the copper ore had to be mined, as stipulated in the contract, being Outani Mine and was for this reason concluded as a result of a mistake, misunderstanding or iustus error, and the second seeking to challenge whether there was consensus between the defendant and the plaintiff regarding the quality of the copper ore which had to be delivered in terms of the said contract.

[7]	The allegations relating to the mistake, misunderstanding or iustus error pertain to the quality of the copper that could be obtained from Outani Mine, for delivery to the plaintiff. The agreement describes the commodity as raw copper with the origin as per certificate of origin to be Namibia, the fineness to be ore, and purity to be tested between five percent and 25 percent with the average of 15 percent copper concentrate. Monthly production as per the agreement had to be ‘5000MT’ per month with the average of plus or minus five percent and sizes had to be ‘19mm’.

[8]	The third parties assert as per the intended amendment that it was objectively impossible for any miner in Namibia to produce copper ore of the purity stipulated in the agreement and that the scenario and the facts on which such an agreement is based is so unlikely that the purported conclusion of the agreement cannot be explained other than that it was based on iustus error, vitiating consensus. Either both the plaintiff and the defendant were mistakenly of the view that it was possible to perform in terms of the agreement, but had they known the true position, they would not have concluded the agreement (thus, they were operating under a common mistake), or there was a unilateral mistake by one or both of them (in the case of both, the mistake would be mutual), the inference sought to be drawn being that the mistake, in either case, must have been caused by culpable conduct or statements of the other party.

[9]	The evidence to support the notion that it was impossible to produce the quality and quantity of the copper ore stipulated in the agreement is set out in various witness statements of the witnesses to be called by the defendant and the third parties, including the expert summary of Dr Harwood and Dr Dixon. It was submitted on behalf of the plaintiff that such evidence would have been objected to as being in conflict with the defendant’s pleadings.

[10]	The plaintiff objects to the proposed amendments by the third parties on the bases that the proposed amendments are sought belatedly, at the advanced stage of the proceedings without an explanation under oath for such lateness. The plaintiff maintains further that the proposed amendments constitute a substantial change of front which will require the plaintiff to revisit the matter from the pleadings stage as well as to amplify its witness statements, expert evidence and discovery. The third basis of the objection is that the evidence is not foreshadowed to support the plea in its intended amended form and lastly that the third parties have not acknowledged liability for costs. Since the objections are similar to those raised against the proposed amendment on behalf of the defendant, I propose to deal with both sets of objections at once, herein below. 

[11]	It is common cause that the defendant was jolted into action after the amendments sought to be made on behalf of the third parties were filed and the defendant’s proposed amendments are modelled on those of the third parties. The defendant, in the first instance seeks to introduce an amendment for the proper construction to be placed on the provisions of the agreement dealing with the quality of the copper ore to be delivered to the plaintiff. The amendment seeks to state that the purity the copper ore would achieve would be between five percent and 25 percent, alternatively an average of 15 percent copper concentrate, once upgraded to copper ore concentrate and that this could be achieved from raw copper ore with the content of about two percent in the ore. 

[12]	In the event of the above not being sustained, and in the alternative, the proposal sought rectification of the agreement, to reflect the above position, but such an attempt at rectification was abandoned and nothing more needs to be said about it.

[13]	The next amendment sought, seeks to introduce a further alternative defence (in the event of the defendant failing to have the defence based on the plea as amended in the first instance sustained), that the agreement as it stands is vitiated by lack of consensus regarding the quality of the copper ore to be delivered to the plaintiff and that such dissensus was caused by a common fundamental mistake that such a quality of ore existed at the Outani Mine and could be delivered, whereas raw copper ore of such quality does not exist at that mine or anywhere else in Namibia and cannot be delivered.

[14]	The final amendment sought to be introduced is that the agreement is unenforceable for being initially impossible (from the inception) to perform, because the quality of copper ore contended by the plaintiff to be what was agreed, cannot be found at the Outani Mine or anywhere else in Namibia.

[15]	Once again the plaintiff objects to the proposed amendments on the bases that they are sought belatedly, at the advance stage of the proceedings after discovery has already been made, witness statements and expert evidence have been filed, and without an explanation under oath why the amendment is sought so late in the proceedings. 

[16]	The objection is also on the bases that the amendment sought will introduce a change of front at a very late stage of the proceedings, which will require the pleadings, witness statements and discovery to be revisited and that no evidence is foreshadowed that will support the defendant’s plea as amended, as per the proposal. It is also said that the amendment will introduce a version which is mutually exclusive to the defences already contained in the defendant’s plea. In this regard, the plaintiff refers to para 6 of the defendant’s plea as it stands, where the defendant admits the written terms of the agreement. According to the plaintiff, the proposed amendment seeks to contradict that admission and will require contradictory evidence, which is impermissible.

[17]	Finally, the objection is also based on failure to tender costs or failure to acknowledge liability for costs.

[18]	For the assertion that an explanation under oath was required due to the belated nature of the amendment sought, the suggestion appears to be that the notice of intention to amend should have been accompanied by an affidavit explaining why the amendment is sought at such a late stage. This objection was taken before the applications to amend, supported by founding affidavits, were filed and the plaintiff persisted in those objection in argument, despite such affidavits having been filed. The argument is not so much that the explanation so provided is inadequate, but that no explanation is provided for the lateness. 

[19]	Both in the objections and the affidavits resisting the amendments, reliance was placed on the decision in Municipal Council of Windhoek v Pioneerspark Dam Investment CC for the proposition that late amendments are subject to greater scrutiny than before because of their deleterious effect upon the administration of justice and that although it is not a prerequisite for an application under rule 52(4) to be accompanied by an affidavit for simple and formal applications, the application for more substantial amendments such as withdrawing an admission or a substantial change of front would need to be done on affidavit.

[20]	I do not understand the above judgment to require that the notice of intention to amend, in terms of rule 52(1) must be accompanied by an affidavit, where the amendment sought is substantial. The judgment refers to rule 52(4) which makes it plain that the affidavit (and thus the explanation under oath) is required at the stage when a party applies to court for an amendment, after an objection is noted against its notice of intention to amend.

[21]	In the present case, both proponents for amendment filed affidavits explaining why amendments are sought at this late stage. The third parties did not initially retain senior counsel, but when the plaintiff, on 29 July 2024 amended its claim by essentially almost doubling the amount claimed from N$52 057 078,89 to N$88 942 503,90, a need was identified to retain senior counsel. The senior counsel so retained studied the record and realised that a defence along the lines of the proposed amendment should be raised and advised accordingly.

[22]	As for the defendant, when the proposed amendment was filed on behalf of the third parties, it was realised that a similar defence should be taken by the defendant. The requirement in the contract relating to the quality of the copper ore to be delivered by the defendant to the plaintiff was already in dispute, as per the existing plea. I refer to paras four and six of the amended particulars of claim and paras two, four, six and nine of the defendant’s plea, as it stands.

[23]	Thus, the intended amendments, in my view, seek to amplify the existing dispute rather than to constitute a complete change of front, and the delay in filing the amendments was explained. I, accordingly, do not agree that there was no explanation under oath for the late amendment and that the proposed amendment by the defendant constitutes a complete change of front or that the third parties seek to introduce completely new defences to the claim. I reject all such bases for the opposition to the proposed amendments.

[24]	As for the objection that the amendment does not raise a triable issue, I also do not agree with the submissions on behalf of the plaintiff. The third parties’ approach in this regard is clearly founded on the record of the documents as they are in the matter, including what is said in the respective witness statements of the parties. If indeed it is established at the trial, - matter which I am not required to decide at this stage, - that performance in terms of the agreement was impossible from the inception because the raw ore quality stipulated in the agreement is impossible to obtain in Namibia - (as asserted on behalf of the third parties and the defendant), - this may well vitiate the agreement. That is a triable issue, for impossibility of performance, in some instances, excuses performance. There is already a version from an expert witnesses, Dr Dixon and Dr Hawood, that this is indeed the case.

[25]	I do not find the version sought to be raised by the third parties to be mere speculation. Even though they are not parties to the agreement, the bases for lack of consensus in initio, which they seek to raise, are from proper inferences to be drawn from what is contained in the agreement, coupled with the evidence of witnesses as contained in the witness statements, that such quality of copper ore cannot be mined in Namibia, except, perhaps, at the Tsumeb Mine. This may result in the court holding that the contract was impossible to perform from the inception. 

[26]	If both the plaintiff and the defendant believed at the time that such quality of ore could be mined at the Outani Mine, and both were mistaken, they were operating under a common mistake in regard to the subject matter of the agreement. This will be the case if the evidence of Dr Dixon holds sway with the court, except, perhaps in the instance that the court finds that the ore could be obtained from the Tsumeb Mine. The agreement indicates that the ore had to be picked up at the ‘Mine site’ but does not seem to define the ‘Mine site’. This and the implications it has for the parties will have to be cleared up by evidence, but my view remains that these are triable issues.

[27]	I also do not see anything mutually exclusive or destructive in the version now sought to be put up by the defendant and what is contained in para 6 of the existing plea. What is clear to me is that the plaintiff and the defendant are in dispute as to the proper construction to be placed on the terms of the agreement describing the quality of the copper ore to be delivered to the plaintiff. That construction will be given by the trial court after hearing evidence and in so far as the plaintiff’s counsel urged me, to at this stage provide an interpretation of that part of the agreement, I decline such an invitation.

[28]	I do so because in the matter of Total Namibia (Pty) Ltd v OBM Engineering and Petroleum Distrubutors CC the Supreme Court, in providing an exposition of the new approach to interpretation, held that the context in which a document is drafted is relevant to its construction in all circumstances and that meaning of words is, to a significant extent, determined by the context in which they are uttered. The Supreme Court went on to hold that 

	‘[23] Again this approach seems to comport with our understanding of the construction of meaning, that context is an important determinant of meaning. It also makes plain that interpretation is 'essentially one unitary exercise' in which both text and context, and in the case of the construction of contracts, at least, the knowledge that the contracting parties had at the time the contract was concluded, are relevant to construing the contract. This unitary approach to interpretation should be followed in Namibia. A word of caution should be noted. In accepting that the distinction between 'background circumstances' and 'surrounding circumstances' should be abandoned, courts should remember that the construction of a contract remains, as Harms JA emphasised in the E KPMG case, 'a matter of law, and not of fact, and accordingly, interpretation is a matter for the court and not for witnesses'. 

[24] The approach adopted here requires a court engaged upon the construction of a contract to assess the meaning, grammar and syntax of the words used, as well as to construe those words within their immediate textual context, as well as against the broader purpose and character of the document itself. Reliance on the broader context will thus not only be resorted to when the meaning of the words viewed in a narrow manner appears ambiguous. Consideration of the background and context will be an important part of all contractual interpretation.’

[29]	It is accordingly clear to me that the proper construction to be placed on the disputed terms of the agreement is a matter for the trial court, to be done after evidence is heard on the surrounding circumstances, the context and the background.

[30]	The objection relating to costs occasioned by the amendment was taken, perhaps without proper application of the mind to the rules applicable to amendments. Rule 52(8) provides that a party giving notice of amendment is, unless the court otherwise orders, liable to pay the costs thereby occasioned to any other party. The plaintiff does not point to any direction to the contrary or why it is of the view that it will otherwise not be entitled to such costs.

[31]	I also agree with the submissions made on behalf of all the parties that such costs are not affected by the provisions of rule 32(11) and are not to be capped. The costs of the application to amend stand on a different footing. They are to be capped in terms of rule 32(11), unless otherwise ordered.

[32]	I also agree with the submission on behalf of all the parties that the court may grant an amendment at any stage of the proceedings, before judgment and also that amendments of pleadings should be allowed in order to obtain a proper ventilation of the dispute between the parties so that justice may be done.

[33]	In my view, both amendments sought should be granted as set out in the respective notices of intention to amend. 

[34]	It is well established that a party seeking an amendment craves an indulgence from the court and should ordinarily bear the costs of amendment, even if successful, unless the opposition was unreasonable. In my view, the amendments sought in the present matter should have been agreed to so as to facilitate progress in the proceedings, which have now been delayed for a period of more than six months. I can however not say that the opposition was unreasonable, considering the stage in the proceedings at which the amendments were sought.

[35]	Even though the pleadings, as sought to be amended, involve complex questions of law, the law relating to amendments is trite and I did not have to traverse new terrain. The costs occasioned by the application to amend should be capped in terms of rule 32(11) and should be granted in favour of the plaintiff in accordance with the general rule that such costs are borne by a party who seeks an indulgence.

[36]	Both the third parties and the defendant indicated, during argument, that they are not liable jointly and severally for costs and that each one should cover only a portion of the costs arising from the opposed application for amendment. I agree. The plaintiff’s costs relating to the hearing of the application for amendment, including the costs relating to heads of argument thereanent should be borne on a 50-50 basis by the third parties on the one hand and the defendant on the other. 

[37]	The costs relating to the pleadings in the respective applications for amendment are separate, because the applications were filed separately, under different interlocutory case numbers. Therefore, the defendant and the third parties must bear such costs, severally. However, the overall costs to be recovered, by the plaintiff must not exceed the cap in terms rule 32(11), in either case.

[38]	The costs in terms of rule 52(8) stand on a different footing and must be borne respectively by the third parties and the defendant.

[39]	Therefore, I make the following order:

The Supreme Court went on to hold that 

	‘[23] Again this approach seems to comport with our understanding of the construction of meaning, that context is an important determinant of meaning. [24] The approach adopted here requires a court engaged upon the construction of a contract to assess the meaning, grammar and syntax of the words used, as well as to construe those words within their immediate textual context, as well as against the broader purpose and character of the document itself. Reliance on the broader context will thus not only be resorted to when the meaning of the words viewed in a narrow manner appears ambiguous. Consideration of the background and context will be an important part of all contractual interpretation.’

[29]	It is accordingly clear to me that the proper construction to be placed on the disputed terms of the agreement is a matter for the trial court, to be done after evidence is heard on the surrounding circumstances, the context and the background.

[31]	I also agree with the submissions made on behalf of all the parties that such costs are not affected by the provisions of rule 32(11) and are not to be capped. [32]	I also agree with the submission on behalf of all the parties that the court may grant an amendment at any stage of the proceedings, before judgment and also that amendments of pleadings should be allowed in order to obtain a proper ventilation of the dispute between the parties so that justice may be done.

[33]	In my view, both amendments sought should be granted as set out in the respective notices of intention to amend. 

[34]	It is well established that a party seeking an amendment craves an indulgence from the court and should ordinarily bear the costs of amendment, even if successful, unless the opposition was unreasonable. I can however not say that the opposition was unreasonable, considering the stage in the proceedings at which the amendments were sought.

[35]	Even though the pleadings, as sought to be amended, involve complex questions of law, the law relating to amendments is trite and I did not have to traverse new terrain. That is a triable issue, for impossibility of performance, in some instances, excuses performance. There is already a version from an expert witnesses, Dr Dixon and Dr Hawood, that this is indeed the case.

[25]	I do not find the version sought to be raised by the third parties to be mere speculation. Even though they are not parties to the agreement, the bases for lack of consensus in initio, which they seek to raise, are from proper inferences to be drawn from what is contained in the agreement, coupled with the evidence of witnesses as contained in the witness statements, that such quality of copper ore cannot be mined in Namibia, except, perhaps, at the Tsumeb Mine. [27]	I also do not see anything mutually exclusive or destructive in the version now sought to be put up by the defendant and what is contained in para 6 of the existing plea. What is clear to me is that the plaintiff and the defendant are in dispute as to the proper construction to be placed on the terms of the agreement describing the quality of the copper ore to be delivered to the plaintiff. [28]	I do so because in the matter of Total Namibia (Pty) Ltd v OBM Engineering and Petroleum Distrubutors CC the Supreme Court, in providing an exposition of the new approach to interpretation, held that the context in which a document is drafted is relevant to its construction in all circumstances and that meaning of words is, to a significant extent, determined by the context in which they are uttered. [31]	I also agree with the submissions made on behalf of all the parties that such costs are not affected by the provisions of rule 32(11) and are not to be capped. [33]	In my view, both amendments sought should be granted as set out in the respective notices of intention to amend. 

[34]	It is well established that a party seeking an amendment craves an indulgence from the court and should ordinarily bear the costs of amendment, even if successful, unless the opposition was unreasonable.
